title: Social media conversions: fix missing and duplicate data
summary: Why social media conversions never match your orders, and how to trace each gap to a missing, duplicate or consent-filtered event before you move budget.
body_markdown:
Your ad dashboard shows more purchases than your order system. GA4 shows fewer. Someone changed checkout last week, but the campaign team also launched new creative. You need to know whether performance changed or the tracking broke before you adjust spend.


Social media conversions need a reconciliation routine, not another dashboard. Start with the transaction, inspect the hits that describe it, and explain why each platform records or credits it differently. Then repeat those checks after every release.


## What a social media conversion counts and where it lives


A social media conversion is a recorded action, such as a purchase, lead or sign-up, that a platform links to an ad or post. The action and the attribution are separate facts. A purchase can exist in your order system without a social platform receiving it or claiming credit.


Say a customer clicks an Instagram ad, returns through search and buys. Your backend records the sale. Other systems receive events about that sale and apply their own identity and attribution rules.


A till receipt shows what was sold, but not which shop window the customer stopped at. In the same way, a transaction record doesn't establish which marketing interaction influenced the purchase.


### Where each system records a social media conversion


The same purchase can appear across these systems. Meta Pixel and CAPI are collection methods feeding Meta, not separate revenue ledgers.


Recording system Where the event fires Identifier used Credit goes to


Meta Pixel Browser, on the confirmation page or purchase hit Browser cookies (` fbp` ,` fbc` ) and` event_id` Meta, when the event can be matched to an account


Conversions API (CAPI) Server, sent from the order system` event_id` , hashed customer fields,` fbc` Meta, where matched events can support attribution


GA4 Browser or server-side tag` client_id` and` transaction_id` Channel grouping under the attribution model set in GA4


Google Ads Conversion tag or offline upload GCLID and enhanced conversion fields The eligible Google click that preceded the conversion


CRM or order backend Order or deal record Order ID and customer email Revenue as the business system records it


Each destination receives the order under its expected event name and identifiers. A renamed purchase event, missing transaction key or altered customer ID can break the connection between records.


Receiving a purchase isn't the same as attributing it.[Meta's CAPI best-practices documentation](https://developers.secure.facebook.com/docs/marketing-api/conversions-api/best-practices) distinguishes basic measurement from attribution and delivery optimization, which require matched events. That distinction matters when a server logs successful delivery but the ad report still looks incomplete.


### Separate recording from credit


Ask which system recorded the action, which channel received credit, and whether social influenced the journey without producing the final click. Don't use the answer to one question as proof of another.


For colleagues building their knowledge of channels and measurement, London School of Business Administration's[self-paced digital marketing course](https://londonsba.org.uk/courses-page/the-credential-of-digital-marketing) provides a broader learning resource alongside hands-on tracking work.


> **Practical rule:** No two totals match by default. Your job is to explain each gap, not force agreement.


## How to investigate a conversion gap


Symptom and likely cause of a conversion gap


Symptom Likely cause Start at step


Platform total above backend orders Browser and server events share no` event_id` 4


Reported purchases jump after a release Event renamed, or retries firing the same event twice 3 and 4


Backend orders above platform total Purchase hit missing, or blocked by consent 3 and 6


Totals close but revenue differs Currency, time zone or order value mismatch 1 and 2


Lead or offline conversion absent in Google Ads GCLID missing, window passed, or wrong action name 7


Event Match Quality falls after a release Hashed email or` fbc` dropped from the server payload 5


These are investigation starting points, not diagnoses. A symptom tells you which evidence to collect first.


A five-step guide infographic for investigating and resolving conversion tracking gaps between different marketing platforms.


### Follow the transaction through the collection path


1.


**Pull the backend order list for the same date window and confirm the time zone each platform uses.** Include order status, currency, value and refunds. The common slip is comparing paid orders with a report that includes cancelled transactions or a different calendar boundary.


2.


**Count purchases per platform for that window and flag any gap above the agreed tolerance.** Compare equivalent actions and revenue definitions. Teams often compare all backend purchases with only the purchases an ad platform attributes to its ads.


3.


**Check the purchase hit in the dataLayer.** Confirm one logical event per transaction, with the expected event name and order ID. Reloading the confirmation page is a useful test because a page-view trigger can accidentally send another purchase.


4.


**Check that Meta Pixel and CAPI send the same` event_name` and` event_id` for each order.** Inspect actual browser and server payloads, not just tag settings. A common slip is generating independent IDs in each collection path.


5.


**Check Event Match Quality and parameter coverage for the recent reporting window.** Inspect server-feed continuity alongside the score. Teams often check whether CAPI accepted the request but overlook missing identity fields.


6.


**Check consent signals on sessions whose completed orders are missing from measurement.** Reproduce the user's choice on the website and inspect the server-side path too. Don't assume that a visible banner proves the tags respected that choice.


7.


**For offline or lead conversions, check the upload timestamp, GCLID and conversion action name.** Keep processing delays separate from rejected uploads. A CRM record marked won doesn't prove that the advertising destination accepted the conversion.


8.


**Send each confirmed cause to the tag or engineering owner with the affected order count and value.** Attach representative hits, the release timestamp and the expected payload. A screenshot of mismatched totals alone rarely gives an engineer enough information to fix the cause.


### Quantify the fault before changing media


Suppose a hypothetical day has 100 backend orders and 130 Meta purchases. That excess points first toward duplicate browser and server events or reporting-scope differences, not better ad performance. Confirm the duplicated order IDs before assigning the cause.

Scheduled checks run daily or weekly, and every finding links the hits it came from.


A clean reconciliation doesn't require identical dashboards. It requires platform, backend and GA4 totals to sit within an agreed tolerance, with a named cause for every material difference that remains.


## Duplicate purchases from Meta Pixel and CAPI


A customer completes a purchase. The browser sends a purchase hit, and the order server sends another. Without aligned deduplication keys, Meta can count them as two conversions. That isn't extra revenue. It's a collection fault that makes acquisition costs look better than they are.


The usual signs are purchases above backend orders, a jump right after a release, or a lower cost per acquisition with no change in spend. They justify an event-level audit; they don't prove duplication on their own. The common causes are concrete:


- **Different event names.** A release renames the browser event but leaves the server event unchanged.
- **Missing order identity.** The backend creates an order ID, but one collection path never receives it.
- **Unstable retry IDs.** A retry generates a fresh identifier, so the repeated purchase looks new.
- **Repeated browser triggers.** A confirmation-page reload sends another purchase with a different key.


[Meta's deduplication documentation](https://business.facebook.com/business/help/1541268312717919) specifies matching` event_name` and identical` event_id` for browser and server events; some configurations can also use matching event names with` external_id` or` fbp` . The event received first is preferred, so timing and retries decide which record remains.


The fix starts in the commerce backend: create one purchase identifier there and pass it unchanged to the dataLayer, the Meta Pixel and CAPI. When the purchase completes outside the website, the CRM handoff needs the same identity; this guide on how to[sync offline conversions with Meta](https://sourceloop.ai/blog/conversion-tracking-facebook-ads/) covers that part. The full diagnosis, with the checks in Events Manager, is in[CAPI deduplication issues](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/capi-deduplication-issues) .


> A successful request proves that a payload arrived. It doesn't prove that the purchase was counted correctly.


## Event match quality and identity gaps


Event Match Quality, or EMQ, measures identity matching, not revenue accuracy.[Meta's EMQ documentation](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/765081237991954/) describes a 0 to 10 score based on customer-information parameters and the share of event instances matched to Meta accounts, evaluated over the most recent 48 hours. That rolling window means the score can lag a broken feed or a repair.


For a conversion gap, EMQ matters in one situation: purchase volume holds, but fewer of those purchases connect to an ad. Suppose EMQ falls after a checkout release. Server purchases stay stable, but the payload no longer carries the hashed email. Compare payloads before and after the release, then inspect the mapping from the checkout form to the order record to the CAPI request. Check normalization before hashing too: hashing a badly formatted email doesn't repair it.


Only check fields where collection and transmission are permitted. A field withheld because the visitor denied consent isn't a defect to work around.


Then sum the backend value of the orders with missing identity fields. That value describes revenue attached to degraded measurement, not proven lost sales. Which parameters weigh most, and how to raise the score, is covered in[Meta event match quality](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/meta-event-match-quality) .


## Missing conversions and Google Ads import limits


A CRM marks a lead as won weeks after the ad click. The sales team sees revenue, but Google Ads shows no corresponding conversion. Before changing attribution settings, inspect when the conversion was uploaded and which import method received it.


[Google's offline import guidance](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15081888?hl=en) states that standard offline conversions uploaded more than 90 days after the last click aren't imported, while enhanced conversions for leads have a 63-day limit; imported conversion statistics can take about three hours to appear. The relevant clock is the associated click, not the date someone reviewed the CRM.


### Import outcome by age of the associated click


These bands describe age eligibility, not a guarantee of acceptance. The upload must also satisfy the conversion action, identifier and customer-data requirements.


Days since last click Standard offline conversion Enhanced conversions for leads


0 to 63 days Imported when the GCLID and conversion action match Imported when the GCLID and hashed customer data match


64 to 90 days Imported when the GCLID and conversion action match Not imported; the enhanced-conversion limit has passed


More than 90 days Not imported and absent from conversion statistics Not imported and absent from conversion statistics


### Separate rejection from processing delay


1. **Confirm the upload timestamp first.** An eligible conversion sitting in a CRM isn't an imported conversion. Inspect the actual submission and its result.
2. **Confirm that the CRM retained the GCLID.** Trace it from the landing session through the form submission and lead record. A field that exists in the CRM schema may still be empty on the affected lead.
3. **Confirm the conversion action.** The upload must reference the intended existing action. Check the submitted name or identifier rather than relying on a label in an export template.
4. **Allow for processing.** A successful upload and a visible reporting total aren't simultaneous. Review upload diagnostics before submitting the same record again.


[Google's enhanced conversions for leads documentation](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15479486) explains how hashed first-party customer information supplements offline measurement. Inspect those fields as well as the click identifier, because incomplete or mismatched customer data can prevent a match.


For a hypothetical lead uploaded 75 days after the click, standard offline import remains age-eligible, but enhanced conversions for leads does not. Closing the deal within a window isn't enough if the upload happens outside it.


If the import succeeds but reports still diverge, use this diagnostic guide to[Google Ads conversions that don't match Analytics](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/google-ads-conversions-dont-match-analytics) to separate collection failures from reporting differences.


## Consent signals that silently remove data


A customer denies advertising consent, completes checkout and still appears in the backend. The advertising report can receive a smaller usable conversion signal. Treat that gap as a possible policy outcome before treating it as a failed purchase event.


The reverse also needs investigation. A banner can record denial while a browser tag or server integration keeps forwarding restricted fields. Start with the symptom: stable backend orders with a lower ad-platform total point toward consent filtering, while denied consent with unchanged outgoing hits points toward leakage.


A person analyzing website analytics on a laptop while holding a smartphone with a consent banner displayed.


### Inspect the signal behind the banner


[Google's Consent Mode reference](https://support.google.com/tagmanager/answer/13802165?hl=en) distinguishes` ad_user_data` , which controls sending user data for advertising and is required for enhanced conversions and tag-based conversion tracking, from` ad_personalization` , which controls personalized advertising. Both must be granted for personalized advertising on Google advertising platforms.


When` ad_user_data` is denied, Google limits some click-ID-keyed conversion exports, including bidding optimization based on Google Analytics conversions. Diagnose that restriction as a consent-state result before suspecting event delivery.


For European Economic Area traffic,[Google's consent requirements](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13695607) also specify these signals and explain that conflicting values disable personalization. Inspect the actual states transmitted by the consent management platform, or CMP, after page load and after the visitor's choice.


### Test the denied path


1. **Confirm the CMP passes the user's choice.** Inspect the consent update payload, then compare it with the selected button.
2. **Check both signal values before advertising tags fire.** Test initial page load and the state after the visitor makes a choice.
3. **Deny consent in a test session.** Follow the journey through checkout and any server-side forwarding.
4. **Inspect restricted data flows.** Confirm that no conversion hit in the denied advertising-data path carries the click ID or customer data that should be withheld.


> A smaller advertising total can be the correct outcome of a respected consent choice.


Document the expected behavior before filing a tracking incident.


When banner behavior and outgoing requests disagree, use this guide to[fix cookie banner issues for accurate tracking](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/fix-cookie-banner-issues-for-accurate-tracking-and-en) . Keep compliant signal loss separate from accidental implementation loss in the reconciliation.


## Confirm the count before bidding learns from it


Pick the platform with the largest unexplained gap. As a practical audit window, review the last 30 days, identify the affected orders and send each confirmed cause to its tag owner with the associated order value.


The tag or engineering owner still owns the fix. A report should identify the failed field, affected release, and expected payload rather than ask someone to investigate tracking.


### Make validation part of release work


Use a repeatable[conversion tracking validation process](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/conversion-tracking-validation) before accepting a release as complete. Test the purchase path, consent states and server retries, then inspect production traffic. A release can pass every spot check and still break a signal that only fires on certain devices or after a consent denial, so production inspection is what confirms the count.


Daily or weekly scheduled checks catch changes in previously dependable signals before teams make further bidding decisions. They don't guarantee detection before every automated bidding cycle, so release QA stays part of the workflow.


Keep the handoff concrete:


- **Evidence.** Attach the browser hit, server payload and affected transaction identifiers.
- **Impact.** State the order count and backend value attached to the fault.
- **Ownership.** Name the person responsible for changing and verifying the setup.


Trackingplan checks the conversion data your campaigns learn from: the requests your website, iOS and Android apps, and server-side endpoints send, with the consent state each one carries. It doesn't bid, manage budgets or change campaigns. It installs as one tag, SDK or server-side hook, and events appear as traffic flows.


Start with that largest gap. Resolve a confirmed cause, verify the corrected hits and keep the check on a schedule. A social media conversion count is only worth bidding on once you can name every difference between it and your orders.
